summary: Across 1,000 simulated futures, buying the $800 laptop changes Alex's median projected balance on 2027-05-01 from $3,281 to $2,481 (middle 80% of futures: $1,942 to $3,034). Alex meets the $1,600 summer housing goal on top of the $1,500 emergency reserve in 8% of futures with the purchase, versus 65% without it. Checking falls below the $200 low-balance line in 97% of futures, versus 6% without it. Total savings dip below the $1,500 emergency reserve in 26% of futures, versus under 1%. In 57% of futures Alex would have to move money out of savings to pay a mandatory bill, versus under 1% without the purchase. On the expected-value path, checking bottoms out at -$26 on 2027-01-01 (baseline: $743).

drivers.label: Lowest checking balance
drivers.detail: In the median future, checking bottoms out at -$39, versus $672 in the baseline.

drivers.label: Summer housing goal
drivers.detail: In the median future, $980 is available for the $1,600 goal on 2027-05-01 after the reserve, versus $1,781.

drivers.label: Busy spending stretch
drivers.detail: The laptop on 2026-09-20 lands at the start of a busy stretch: everyday spending through 2026-10-03 is expected to be $319, versus $260 in an average stretch of the year (groceries 1.26×, discretionary 1.19× their usual). This happens with or without the purchase.

drivers.label: Expected income
drivers.detail: $11,520 of expected income through 2027-05-01 rebuilds the balance in both scenarios.

assumptions: Precomputed result: generated by the Monte Carlo simulator (seed 1) for this $800 laptop request; it does not respond to other requests.
Monte Carlo over 1,000 simulated futures. In each future, the baseline and the purchase scenario share the same sampled income and spending.
Balances are medians across simulated futures. Probabilities are the share of futures in which the event happens.
Each paycheck is drawn independently from a normal distribution around its expected amount, using the twin's per-payment uncertainty, kept within 3 standard deviations and never below $0.

Spending in each category is drawn independently for every 14-day period from a normal distribution using the twin's mean and standard deviation, spread evenly over the period and never below $0 (which raises average spending slightly).

A category with a seasonal pattern has its average and spread scaled for each 14-day period by the months that period covers (a period spanning two months blends them); over a full year it averages to the twin's figure.
Groceries spending is highest in January (1.63× an average fortnight) and lowest in July (0.60×).
Discretionary spending is highest in December (2.34× an average fortnight) and lowest in April (0.49×).
Bill amounts, bill due dates, and paycheck dates are fixed; bill confidence is not used.
A mandatory bill checking cannot cover is paid by moving money from savings, even if that breaks the emergency reserve; it counts as uncovered only when checking and savings together fall short.
Everyday spending and optional charges are never paid from savings.
Low balance means checking below $200 (default; Alex has not set a minimum).
The emergency reserve counts checking plus savings.
Goals must be met on top of the emergency reserve.
Income, bills, and everyday spending all flow through checking.
Every recurring bill, including optional ones, is charged in full.
